title: What is an AI assistant for event lead capture?
summary: An AI assistant for event lead capture answers questions about your leads and CRM pipeline in plain language. See how it compares to other assistants for events.
body_text: Every marketing team has an AI assistant in the mix now. You brief ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini, connect it to your data, and hand off the work you used to grind through by hand. Event teams are no different, and on the show floor AI assistants have already arrived. One reads badges the moment they're scanned. Another helps you work the room from the organizer's event app. And a third books the follow-up before you've left the hall. As the platforms behind events get smarter, a newer kind is taking shape: the AI assistant for event lead capture. It earns its keep across the three moments that decide whether a show paid off. You walk in with a target list. You reach the hottest leads before they cool. And when leadership asks whether the booth was worth it, you show the pipeline instead of a week of spreadsheet cleanup. Keep reading for a breakdown of the AI assistants for events in 2026, and what to weigh when you're choosing one for event lead capture . What are AI assistants for events? "AI for events" has turned into a catch-all. It gets stamped on tools that do very different jobs, which is how two products can both call themselves "AI-powered" and share almost nothing under the hood. Before you can choose the right one, it helps to see the whole landscape. The AI assistants showing up at events today sort into five types, each built for a different part of the job . Type of AI assistant What it does Example Capture-time AI Reads badges and business cards, then enriches and/or scores each lead automatically momencio IntelliSense, MLeads, Popl Universal Badge Scanner Conversation capture Records and summarizes the booth conversation and attaches it to the lead Blinq AI Notetaker, BoothIQ Event-app assistants Help attendees and exhibitors find their way around one organizer's event Swapcard Sherlock, Eventdex AI Agent Meeting and follow-up automation Books meetings and sends follow-up messages after the show CalendarBridge, Popl Event Flows Lead capture assistants Answer questions about the leads you captured and your CRM pipeline, inside the AI tool you already use Ask Popl The reason the label gets confusing is that all five wear it. A badge scanner that reads text off a business card gets called "AI for events," and so does an assistant you can hold a full conversation with about your pipeline. Same words, completely different tools. The type worth zooming in on is the last one. What is an AI assistant for event lead capture? An AI assistant for event lead capture is a conversational tool that connects to both the leads you capture at an event and the CRM those leads sync to, then answers questions about them in plain language. Instead of building a report, you ask a question and get an answer drawn from your own data. What sets this type apart from the other four is range. Each of the others handles one slice of the event: a badge, a booth conversation, a single show, or the follow-up. An AI assistant for event lead capture is the one you actually talk to, and it reads across all of it: the leads, the notes your reps took on the floor, the answers to your qualifying questions, and how each lead progressed through your CRM pipeline. AI assistants for event lead capture are the newest of the five. Popl just released one called Ask Popl . Since "AI" gets stamped on all kinds of tools, ROI-focused event marketers will want to know what sets an AI assistant for event lead capture apart from the rest. How does an AI assistant for event lead capture work? An AI assistant for event lead capture works by connecting to two things: the leads you capture on the show floor, and the CRM those leads flow into. Once it's connected, you ask it questions in plain language, and it answers from that live data with no report to build first. The connection runs on something called the Model Context Protocol , an open standard that lets an AI tool pull live data from another system through a secure, permissioned link. You don't need to follow the technical setup, only the difference it makes in your day-to-day. Here's what that difference looks like. Picture the two ways you might put event leads in front of Claude. You could export them to a spreadsheet and paste them in. That works once, but you've handed it a snapshot frozen at the moment you hit export, and next week you're exporting again . Or the AI assistant connects to your lead capture platform and, through it, your CRM, then reads the current records every time you ask. Same question, but now the answer reflects what's true today, and you can ask it again after the next show without touching a spreadsheet. What can you ask an AI assistant for event lead capture? The clearest way to understand an AI assistant for event lead capture is to look at what you'd actually ask it. Most teams reach for it at three points in an event: before the show, right after it, and when it's time to report. For example, here's what each use case looks like with Popl's AI assistant for event lead capture, Ask Popl: Before the show: build a target list Tell it which show you're attending and describe the buyer you want to meet, and it comes back with real contacts at the companies exhibiting. What makes this work is how little it needs to go on: Popl's enrichment can build a full record from a name and company, a name and job title, a name and location, or just a LinkedIn profile, where most tools need a name and a company to start. Ask Popl hands you a ready-to-send CSV of those enriched contacts, so the list is ready to work the moment you get it instead of sitting in a chat window. This pre-show research runs on Event Intelligence , Popl's feature for finding and enriching prospects before you reach the floor. After the show: decide who to work first Ask it to read the notes and qualifying answers across everything your team captured, and rank the leads by fit. Instead of 400 rows sorted by scan time, you get a prioritized list of who to reach first. It's just as useful for catching what's slipping: the leads nobody has followed up since the last show, or a rep whose pipeline has gone quiet. At reporting time: justify every event dollar Ask it to line up the leads you captured against your CRM pipeline, and you get the report without building it: pipeline generated, open opportunities, closed-won revenue, broken out by event and by rep. When Ask this What you get back Before the show "I'm exhibiting at [show]. Find decision-makers in [role] at the companies exhibiting, and enrich them." A ready-to-send CSV of enriched target contacts After the show "Read the notes and qualifying answers from [event] and rank the leads by fit." A prioritized list of who to work first — plus leads going cold At reporting time "Match the leads we captured at [event] to our CRM pipeline. Show pipeline, open opps, and closed-won by rep." An event-ROI report without building a spreadsheet Josh Schwartz, VP of Marketing and Demand Generation at Element451, put his Popl and HubSpot data in one Claude conversation and shaved hours off his end-of-quarter reporting. How does an AI assistant for event lead capture compare to the alternatives? For years, lead capture tools competed on one thing: how fast they could scan a badge. That race is over. The platforms behind events now compete on what happens after the scan, whether that means enriching the record, scoring the lead, or answering a question about it. That shift is why "AI for events" now covers so many tools, and why choosing one means knowing what each is actually built to do. Of the five types above, the lead capture assistant is the one you talk to about your leads and your pipeline. It isn't the only way a team tries to get those answers, though. When you're choosing one, here are the realistic alternatives you're weighing, and the different problem each solves. CRM-native AI connectors. HubSpot and Salesforce now ship their own AI connectors that read and write CRM data in plain language. They're genuinely useful for pipeline questions. What they can't see is how a record came to exist: the booth conversation, the qualifying answers, which rep scanned the badge, what enrichment added. None of that lives in the CRM unless something put it there. They answer pipeline questions, not event questions, and they pair well with a capture platform that feeds them. Popl syncs into both. Event-app AI. Organizer platforms like Swapcard build capable assistants into their apps. On the exhibitor side they can rank attendees by intent and search the attendee list by ICP. The catch is scope: the organizer turns it on, not you, and it only knows the one show it lives inside. It can make a single event workable. It can't tell you how your spring shows compared to your fall ones, because it never sees them. Capture-tool AI. Some capture apps, like momencio, run AI inside their own dashboard that decides which leads matter and how they're scored, automatically. That helps if you want the tool to make the call for you. It's a different thing from an assistant you can question: it decides what data to surface, not you. A general AI tool plus a CSV export. The honest baseline. For one show and one straightforward question, exporting your leads and pasting them into Claude or ChatGPT works fine. The limits show up the second time you ask: it's a snapshot frozen at the moment you exported, it doesn't reconcile against what your CRM knows, and repeating it next quarter means redoing the whole export. Workflow automation. Tools like Popl Event Flows aren't really an alternative here; they're the layer underneath. They route leads, trigger follow-up, and lock attribution the moment a badge is scanned, which is what makes the data trustworthy in the first place. They keep the record clean and moving. They showcase real-time attribution data but don’t engage in a conversation with you about it. Approach What it can see Data freshness Scope Who turns it on The problem it solves Lead capture assistant (e.g., Ask Popl) Capture layer and CRM Live Across all your events Your team Answering questions about your leads and pipeline in plain language CRM-native AI connector (HubSpot, Salesforce) The CRM record only Live Whatever's in the CRM Your admin Pipeline questions, once the data is already in the CRM Event-app AI (e.g., Swapcard) One show's attendee data Live, during the show A single event The organizer Working the room at one specific event Capture-tool AI (e.g., momencio, Popl) Leads inside its own dashboard Live, in-app Its own captured leads Your team Auto-enriching or scoring leads without you asking General AI tool + CSV export Whatever you exported Snapshot Whatever's in the file You A one-off question about one show Workflow automation (e.g., Event Flows) Leads as they're captured Live Across events Your team Routing, attribution, and follow-up so the data stays clean What to look for in an AI assistant for event lead capture in 2026 You don't need to read a vendor's technical docs to tell these tools apart . A short list of questions does it, and each one is fair to ask in a demo. What to weigh Why it matters Worth asking Live data, or a static file A tool that reads your live records answers with what's true today, and you can re-ask it after the next show. One working from an upload is frozen the moment you exported. "Does it read our records directly, or work from a file we upload each time?" What it can see: leads, CRM, or both Event questions (who we met, what the rep noted) need the capture layer. Pipeline questions need the CRM. Proving ROI needs both. This is the biggest factor in which questions it can answer. "Can it see both the leads we capture and how they move through our CRM?" Reads only, or writes back too Writing to your CRM is useful, but worth guardrails. A tool that reaches your CRM through your capture platform stays inside that platform's field mapping, duplicate checks, and sync history, so a wrong write is less likely and easier to trace. "If it can change our data, what sits between it and the CRM?" Who turns it on Whether an admin switches it on once for the team or each person connects their own login changes your security review and who can actually use it. "Does an admin enable it for the team, or does everyone connect individually?" What your plan includes Specific plans, CRM tiers, or the organizer permissions may be required to use an AI assistant for event lead capture. "Is this on our plan, or does it need an upgrade, a certain CRM tier, or the organizer to switch it on?" One event, or all of them Portfolio questions like, “How did our spring shows compare to fall?” need a tool that sees every event, not one show at a time. "Can it compare across all our events, or only one show at a time?" Do you need an AI assistant for event lead capture? Whether or not you need an AI assistant for event lead capture depends on your event program. An AI assistant for event lead capture earns its place when you have a full event calendar, data you trust, and revenue goals . Here are four situations that call for one: You have a full event calendar Volume and repetition are exactly what an assistant is built for: dozens of shows a year, hundreds of leads at a time, the same questions after every one. That's the point where reading the list by hand stops scaling and asking your data directly starts saving real hours. The flip side is a single small show. If fourteen leads fit on one screen, you can spot the three that matter and follow up by lunch. Your capture data is clean and connected An assistant answers confidently from whatever it's given, so complete records and attribution locked at scan are what let it answer accurately. When the inputs are sound, you get answers you can act on. When they aren't, you get confident answers built on blank fields, mismatched CRM records, and attribution gaps. The fix is clean capture first: enrichment that fills the record and attribution locked the moment a badge is scanned. Get the inputs right, then the assistant has something real to read. Your questions are the kind a conversation answers Which leads should we call first? Who captured the most leads? How much pipeline did the event generate? An AI assistant handles these well, and they're the questions that tie events to revenue. Where it stops is the questions that need real number-crunching underneath. Say you want to know how many of those deals you'd have closed even if you'd skipped the show, or how to split credit for one sale across every touch that led to it, from the booth to the webinar to the follow-up calls. That's an analyst's job, and dressing it up as a plain-language question invites a confident answer with none of the rigor underneath. When the stakes justify that rigor, reach for a data team, not a chat window. You need automated workflows An assistant is for asking: it tells you a rep's pipeline went quiet or which leads are going cold. It doesn't route a lead, trigger a follow-up, or assign an owner the second a badge is scanned. That's automation's job, and the two work best together: automation keeps the pipeline moving, the assistant tells you what's happening in it. When your calendar is full, your capture data is sound, and your questions are the kind you'd ask out loud, an AI assistant for event lead capture earns its place. What an AI assistant could do for your event workflow You're not short on AI tools these days. The modern event team runs on a growing set of assistants, each built for a different stretch of the show. The one for event lead capture is the one you actually hold a conversation with, and its real value is range: it stays with you from the first target list to the final ROI number, always in plain language. Where it shines is before the doors even open. Tell it which show you're working and the buyers you want to meet, and it comes back with real, enriched contacts to prospect. That’s the kind of pre-show legwork that used to cost you an afternoon. From there, the same assistant keeps paying off: surfacing the leads worth calling first while they're still warm, then running revenue attribution once the booth is packed and leadership wants ROI numbers. Curious how an AI assistant could streamline your event workflow? Head over to Popl’s AI prompt library to explore use cases from prospecting exhibitor lists to comparing performance across events. Frequently asked questions What is an AI assistant for event lead capture? An AI assistant for event lead capture is a conversational tool that connects to both your in-person lead capture platform and the CRM those leads sync to, then answers questions about them in plain language. Instead of building a report, you ask a question and get an answer drawn from your own data. It is the newest of the AI tools marketed for events, and the only one you can hold a conversation with. Ask Popl is one example. What's the difference between an AI assistant and AI lead scoring? The difference between an AI assistant and AI lead scoring is who starts the conversation. Lead scoring decides for you, assigning each lead a number automatically inside the tool that captured it, whether or not you asked. An AI assistant waits for your question and answers it from your data, including things nobody built a scoring field for. Scoring hands you a ranking; an assistant lets you ask why, compare events, or pull unique insights. The two solve different problems and often work well together. Does an AI assistant for event lead capture need access to my CRM? An AI assistant for event lead capture needs your CRM only for the money questions. Telling you who you captured, what they said at the booth, or which rep worked them takes only your event data. Telling you what those leads became takes your CRM, because pipeline, open deals, and closed revenue all live there. Can an AI assistant for event lead capture write back to my CRM? Some AI assistants can write back to your CRM, and the bigger question is what controls the write. Usually records reach your CRM through your lead capture platform's existing connection, not a direct line from the AI tool, so any write follows that platform's rules. Ask Popl is one example: an admin sets which fields can be written, duplicates are caught on email and phone, and every change is logged. Before switching on any write path, confirm what you can control and what you can audit. Can ChatGPT or Claude analyze my event leads? Yes, ChatGPT or Claude can analyze your event leads, in one of two ways. You can export the leads to a spreadsheet and paste them in, which works once but freezes the data at the moment you exported. Or you can connect your lead capture platform so the AI tool reads your live records each time you ask, with no new export. Ask Popl uses the second method, connecting your Popl and CRM data to Claude, ChatGPT, or Microsoft Copilot. What does an AI assistant for event lead capture cost? The cost of an AI assistant for event lead capture usually depends on the platform it belongs to, since most are a feature of a lead capture or CRM product rather than a standalone purchase. Access often comes with a specific plan or tier instead of a separate price tag. Ask Popl, for example, is included on Popl's Event Lead Capture plan, so teams already on that plan use it at no added cost. Is my data safe with an AI assistant for event lead capture? Whether your data is safe with an AI assistant for event lead capture comes down to a few things worth checking: whose permissions it borrows, where it runs, what it is allowed to see, and how the vendor is audited. A well-built assistant reads only the data you already have access to, through a connection an admin approves. Ask Popl works this way — and it runs inside Popl, which is SOC 2 Type II attested for the Security criterion, hosts data in the U.S., publishes its DPA and subprocessor list, and commits contractually to breach notification within 72 hours.

From Screen to Stitch: Sybylla's Cardigan From ‘My Brilliant Career’ Is Yours to Knit
summary: Inspired by the on-screen writing cardigan worn by Sybylla, 'My Brilliant Career's' fiercely ambitious heroine, Netflix has teamed up with female-owned knitwear label Cardigang to release a free knitting pattern
body_text: Inspired by the on-screen writing cardigan worn by Sybylla, My Brilliant Career 's fiercely ambitious heroine, Netflix has teamed up with female-owned knitwear label Cardigang to release a free knitting pattern so fans can knit a piece of the story for themselves. Fans of My Brilliant Career who've watched Sybylla Melvyn (Philippa Northeast) write, dream and defy convention in her signature pink cardigan can now knit their own. Netflix has partnered with Cardigang to release The Sybylla - a free pattern inspired by Sybylla's hero writing cardigan - available to download from today. Oversized, threaded with soft silk ribbon and pulled on every time Sybylla puts pen to paper, the cardigan serves as Sybylla’s creative permission slip. Cardigang has paid homage to it with its own simplified pattern, inspired by the piece's silhouette and spirit - tested from cast-on to bind-off. Whether you've been knitting for years or are picking up needles for the very first time, this one's made for you. "Everything shifts for Sybylla when she arrives at Five Bob Downs and falls under Augusta's spell,” said Mariot Kerr, costume designer on My Brilliant Career . "Through her, Sybylla begins to see that intelligence, creativity and boldness can pair beautifully with style." "The writing cardigan had to feel like something Augusta herself would give to Sybylla — generous, glamorous and a little whimsical, while also warm, comforting and nurturing. Oversized and threaded with soft silk ribbons, it creates a cocoon where Sybylla can write, dream and discover her own voice." Want everything you need to make The Sybylla in one go? Cardigang's kit has you covered with the needles, yarn and pattern together, available from Cardigang's website. Download the pattern PDF HERE or shop the kit at Cardigang . Now it's your turn to knit your own brilliant career - let's get started! Share your progress and finished cardigans by tagging @NetflixANZ, @cardigang_knits and #MyBrilliantCareer .

title: Runway Growth Finance Corp. Reports Second Quarter 2026 Financial Results
summary: Delivered Total and Net Investment Income of $37.0 million and $18.2 million, Respectively Investment Portfolio of $1.2 billion Conference Call on Friday, August 7, 2026 at 10:00 a.m. ET MENLO PARK, Calif., Aug. 06, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Runway Growth Finance Corp.
body_text: Release Details Runway Growth Finance Corp. Reports Second Quarter 2026 Financial Results August 6, 2026 PDF Version Delivered Total and Net Investment Income of $37.0 million and $18.2 million, Respectively Investment Portfolio of $1.2 billion Conference Call on Friday, August 7, 2026 at 10:00 a.m. ET MENLO PARK, Calif., Aug. 06, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Runway Growth Finance Corp. (Nasdaq: RWAY) (“Runway Growth” or the “Company”), a leading provider of flexible capital solutions to late- and growth-stage companies seeking an alternative to raising equity, today announced its financial results for the second quarter ended June 30, 2026. Second Quarter 2026 Highlights Total investment portfolio of $1.2 billion at fair value Total investment income of $37.0 million Net investment income of $18.2 million, or $0.43 per share Net asset value of $502.6 million, or $11.91 per share Dollar-weighted annualized yield on debt investments of 14.2% Funded approximately $239.6 million of investments acquired in connection with the Company's acquisition of SWK Holdings, including $216.2 million across 13 acquired loan positions and $23.4 million in acquired equity positions, with a combination of cash and the Company's common stock as consideration Ten investments completed in new and existing portfolio companies, representing $101.7 million in funded investments, which net of assignments was $85.8 million Aggregate proceeds of $36.5 million, representing $15.9 million in assignments, $10.5 million from scheduled repayments, and $10.1 million in sale proceeds from equity Repurchased 249,169 shares during the quarter for an aggregate purchase price of $1.4 million Third Quarter 2026 Distributions Declared third quarter 2026 dividend of $0.33 per share “During the second quarter, we made meaningful progress executing our strategy while further strengthening the foundation of the business,” said David Spreng, Founder and Co-Chief Executive Officer of Runway Growth. “The successful integration of the SWK portfolio has enhanced our diversification, increased our earnings capacity and broadened our opportunity set. At the same time, we remain disciplined in our capital allocation, balancing new investments with opportunistic share repurchases. Complementing these efforts, our investment adviser and its affiliates recently announced their commitment to purchase up to 10% of our outstanding shares. Together, these actions reflect strong alignment with our shareholders and confidence in Runway’s long-term value.” “I also want to welcome Mike Rovner, who has been appointed Co-Chief Executive Officer of Runway Growth Finance and Co-Chief Investment Officer of Runway Growth Capital,” continued Mr. Spreng. “Mike brings more than 30 years of experience spanning technology, venture capital, private credit and growth lending. His experience building and leading investment platforms, together with his connectivity across the BC Partners platform, further strengthens our leadership team and investment capabilities. Mike's disciplined investment philosophy and deep understanding of the innovation economy closely align with the culture we've built at Runway, and I look forward to partnering with him as we remain focused on maximizing shareholder returns.” Second Quarter 2026 Operating Results Total investment income for the quarter ended June 30, 2026 was $37.0 million, compared to $35.1 million for the quarter ended June 30, 2025. The Company's dollar-weighted annualized yield on average debt investments for the quarter ended June 30, 2026 was 14.2%. The yield was modestly impacted by the transition of BlueShift and Marley Spoon to non-accrual status at the end of the first quarter. The Company calculates the yield on dollar-weighted debt investments for any period measured as (1) total investment-related income during the period divided by (2) the daily average of the fair value of debt investments, including investments on non-accrual status, outstanding during the period. Total operating expenses for the quarter ended June 30, 2026 were $18.8 million, compared to $21.2 million for the quarter ended June 30, 2025. Net investment income for the quarter ended June 30, 2026 was $18.2 million, or $0.43 per share, compared to $13.9 million, or $0.38 per share, for the quarter ended June 30, 2025. Net realized loss was $45.3 million for the quarter ended June 30, 2026, compared to a net realized loss of $1.5 million for the quarter ended June 30, 2025. For the quarter ended June 30, 2026, net change in unrealized gain was $54.3 million, compared to a net change in unrealized gain of $4.4 million for the quarter ended June 30, 2025. For the quarter ended June 30, 2026, our net increase in net assets resulting from operations was $27.2 million, or $0.65 per share, compared to a net increase in net assets resulting from operations of $16.8 million, or $0.45 per share, for the quarter ended June 30, 2025. Portfolio and Investment Activity As of June 30, 2026, Runway Growth’s investment portfolio had an aggregate fair value of $1.2 billion in 79 companies, comprising $1.1 billion in loans, 98.0% of which are senior secured loans, and $70.0 million in warrants and other equity-related investments. During the second quarter of 2026, Runway Growth funded approximately $239.6 million of investments acquired in connection with the Company's acquisition of SWK Holdings, including $216.2 million across 13 acquired loan positions and $23.4 million in acquired equity positions, with a combination of cash and the Company's common stock as consideration, which net of the purchase discount was $225.2 million. The Company also completed ten investments in new and existing portfolio companies, representing $101.7 million in funded investments, which net of assignments was $85.8 million. Total debt and equity fundings net of upfront loan origination fees and purchase discounts were $325.4 million. During the second quarter of 2026, Runway Growth received aggregate proceeds of $26.0 million in principal prepayments and equity sale proceeds. In addition, Runway Growth received proceeds of $10.5 million in scheduled amortizations. Total portfolio investment activity for the three months ended June 30, 2026 and 2025 was as follows: Three Months Ended June 30, 2026 2025 Beginning investment portfolio $ 886,346 $ 1,004,233 Purchases of investments 325,352 38,719 PIK interest 1,957 4,093 Sales and prepayments of investments (25,974 ) (25,000 ) Scheduled repayments of investments (10,469 ) (4,230 ) Amortization of fixed income premiums or accretion of discounts 5,330 2,917 Net realized gain (loss) on investments (44,384 ) (1,501 ) Net change in unrealized gain (loss) on investments 54,192 5,720 Ending investment portfolio $ 1,192,350 $ 1,024,951 Net Asset Value As of June 30, 2026, net asset value per share was $11.91, compared to $12.13 as of March 31, 2026. Total net assets at the end of the second quarter of 2026 was $502.6 million, an increase of 15% from $438.2 million as of March 31, 2026. Liquidity and Capital Resources As of June 30, 2026, the Company had approximately $210.8 million in available liquidity, including unrestricted cash and cash equivalents of $10.8 million and $200.0 million in available borrowing capacity under the Company’s credit facility, subject to existing terms, advance rates and regulatory and covenant requirements. The Company ended the quarter with a core leverage ratio of approximately 136%, compared to 98% for the quarter ended March 31, 2026. Distributions On August 5, 2026, the Company’s board of directors (the "Board of Directors") declared a quarterly distribution of $0.33 per share for stockholders of record as of August 17, 2026. Distributions are payable on August 31, 2026. Recent Developments The Company evaluated events subsequent to June 30, 2026 through August 6, 2026, the date the consolidated financial statements were issued. There have been no subsequent events that occurred during such period that would require recognition or disclosure, except as disclosed below. Credit Facility On July 13, 2026, the Company entered into the Eighth Amendment to its amended and restated credit agreement (the “Credit Facility Amendment”). The Credit Facility Amendment, (i) reduced the total commitments under the Credit Facility from $550.0 million to $425.0 million; (ii) permitted the future prepayment and termination of a certain lender’s commitments on a non-pro rata basis; (iii) amended certain financial covenants; (iv) updated certain key-person trigger events; and (v) amended certain loan eligibility criteria and borrowing-base concentration limitations. Appointment of Co-Chief Executive Officer On August 5, 2026, the Board of Directors elected Michael Rovner, age 56, as the Company’s Co-Chief Executive Officer, effective as of the close of business on August 6, 2026 (the “Effective Time”), to serve alongside R. David Spreng, whose title will change from Chief Executive Officer and President to Co-Chief Executive Officer and President of the Company, as of the Effective Time. In addition, Mr. Rovner will serve as the Co-Chief Executive Officer, the Co-Chief Investment Officer and as a member of the investment committee of Runway Growth Capital LLC ("RGC"), effective as of the Effective Time. Mr. Rovner has more than 30 years of industry experience spanning early and growth stage technology companies, private equity, private credit, and growth-debt lending. Prior to joining the Company, Mr. Rovner served as a managing director at BC Partners and its affiliate Mount Logan Management since 2023. Before that, from 2012 to 2023, he served as the chief executive officer and head of the investment committee of Ovation Partners, a provider of asset backed lending solutions and growth capital for established companies, which he co-founded. From 2009 to 2011, Mr. Rovner served on the Board of Directors of Vida Capital, a vertically integrated manager of insurance-related and longevity contingent assets, which he co-founded in 2009. From 2000 to 2011, he served as a partner and head of the financial services practice of Austin Ventures, a venture capital and growth equity firm focused on early-stage and growth equity investments in the financial services, technology, digital media, and technology-enabled services markets. Mr. Rovner began his career in early-stage technology businesses, including Empart Technology (acquired by ARI Networks), Stanford Technology Group (acquired by Informix Software), and Mission Critical Software (NASDAQ IPO and subsequent acquisition by NetIQ Corporation). Mr. Rovner received a B.A. in English from UCLA. Investment Committee Effective as of the close of business on August 6, 2026, RGC’s Investment Committee will consist of R. David Spreng, Michael Rovner, Thomas B. Raterman and Patrick Schafer. For additional information regarding Mr. Rovner’s appointment and the related changes to RGC’s Investment Committee, refer to the Company’s Quarterly Report on Form 10-Q for the quarter ended June 30, 2026, being filed concurrently with this Current Report on Form 8-K. Recent Portfolio Activity From July 1, 2026 through August 6, 2026, the Company funded $1.9 million in unfunded commitments on existing investments. The Company also received $17.1 million in debt prepayments. Conference Call Runway Growth will hold a conference call to discuss its second quarter ended June 30, 2026 financial results at 7:00 a.m. PT (10:00 a.m. ET) on Friday, August 7, 2026. To participate in the conference call or webcast, participants should register online at the Runway Investor Relations website . The earnings call can also be accessed through the following links: Conference Call Webcast A live webcast will be available in the investor section of the Company’s website , and will be archived for 90 days following the call. body_text: Michael Burry launched a paid newsletter in late 2025, and within months, it was the #8 most-subscribed publication across all Brex customers, racing ahead of writers who spent a decade building their base. A two-decade-old reputation for contrarian calls became a line item on startup corporate cards in a matter of months. That's what this Brex Benchmark measures: the reading that survives an expense report. A decade ago, a founder's market intelligence was free: TechCrunch for funding news, Hacker News for technical arguments, Twitter for everything else. You could read all of it and still not know what to do on Monday. Free media is paid by the size of its audience, which makes it very good at telling you what happened and useless at telling you what to do. Today the operating knowledge lives behind paywalls, attached to specific names. Product-market fit questions go to Lenny's. Engineering org problems go to The Pragmatic Engineer. A platform shift sends you to Stratechery. The newsletter stack has become part of company formation, as standard as the SaaS stack. While a personal subscription means you like something, a company subscription that gets expensed, approved, and renewed means it helps run your business. And because Brex's card data identifies the publication behind each charge, not just the billing platform, these rankings follow the writer, whether they publish on Substack, Ghost, beehiiv, or their own site. Across Brex customers, those renewals add up to the startup economy's required reading list. Trend 1: The winners stopped selling newsletters and started selling memberships. The complaint about the newsletter boom is fatigue: too many sends, a few names absorbing everyone else's growth. But fatigue is an inbox problem, and the winners left the inbox. Lenny's comes with a 30,000-person Slack and software credits. Stratechery is a daily column plus four podcasts. Unsubscribing from an email costs nothing; leaving a room with 30,000 people in it costs something. The same three names have led this list since a year ago, and they cover the three functions every company staffs first: Lenny Rachitsky on product, Gergely Orosz on engineering, Ben Thompson on strategy. Among Brex customers, these are the subscriptions a company expenses without a second thought, the way an earlier generation expensed trade magazines. Thompson predicted why value would flow to individual writers back in 2014, in Publishers and the Smiling Curve: value in internet media flows to the two ends of the chain, aggregators on one side and 'focused, responsive, and differentiated' writers on the other. The middle is missing from this newsletter list. Nearly every entry is one writer or a small team who owns a subject. The leaders are still growing. Lenny's has more paid subscribers on Brex than #2 and #3 combined, and all three grew double digits, led by The Pragmatic Engineer at +36%. Engineering was where the money went in 2025; the reading budget followed. The Free Press is the one entry that isn't a single writer’s judgment business. It climbed to #4, up 93% on Brex cards, and it scaled by selling: Paramount bought it for $150 million and put Bari Weiss in charge of CBS News. One writer's judgment scales on a laptop; a newsroom needs a payroll. That may be why the only newsroom on this list is also the only entry that got acquired. One rung below, Emily Sundberg's Feed Me is up 38%. Feed Me is a read about taste and consumer culture, and it sits four spots below Stratechery on the same corporate cards. Trend 2: Startups will pay to be told they might be wrong. Burry made his name being right about the 2008 crash after years of being told he was wrong, then spent two decades communicating in fragments. The newsletter reverses that: for the first time, his research is available to anyone with a subscription. Startups buy it for the same reason anyone buys research. Every company needs a view on AI, rates, and capital right now, and Burry offers a track record of being early and a habit of not caring who disagrees. Most subscribers probably don't think he's right, but they want to know early if he is. Two decades of credibility, and the market found it within months of launch. Startups pay for writers who can make them re-examine the default story. Trend 3: A healthcare-interoperability newsletter cracked the top 15. Brendan Keeler's Health API Guy, a newsletter about healthcare interoperability, debuted at #13 — and Christina Farr's Second Opinion jumped to #10, up 56%. An interoperability newsletter cracking a top-15 business reading list means a vertical is producing real companies. Once enough startups build in a category, general tech media is too broad and industry trade news is too shallow, and the person who knows the info becomes valuable. The economics reward this: a niche audience that needs the information pays more reliably than a broad one that merely enjoys it. The pattern repeats across the list: Thesis Driven for real estate, Bankless for crypto, This Week in Fintech for financial services. A vertical read climbing this list is an early signal that companies in that vertical are forming and spending. Just below the top 15, Fintech Business Weekly gives financial services a second dedicated read, and Chipstrat sits right behind it. Founders are now budgeting to understand semiconductor supply. Why startups pay to read A business prices a purchase against the money it makes or saves, and in Brex data newsletter subscriptions behave accordingly. In Brex data, they get bought the way software gets bought: approved, renewed, carried from one budget cycle to the next. A few hundred dollars a year competes with the cost of a bad hire, a mispriced round, or a product bet made blind. If it improves a single decision, one hire, one pricing call, one product bet, it has covered a decade of renewals. Fifteen writers, most of them working alone, are now a standing line item at tens of thousands of companies. What startups buy tells you what they think they don't know. For the companion piece on what startups are reading in book form, see Brex Benchmark: The 25 books founders are reading in 2026 Methodology and privacy Sumeet Marwaha is the Head of Data at Brex, supporting Brex in understanding how customers spend, adopt tools, and grow their businesses. We pulled paid newsletter subscriptions across all Brex customers, anonymized and aggregated, and compared October 2025 through June 2026 against the same nine months a year earlier. Brex's L2/L3 card data identifies the publication behind a charge rather than just the billing platform, so we can see past "Substack spend went up" to the individual writers getting paid. Descriptor detail varies by platform; the rankings are a floor, not a census. We publish rankings, rank movement, and percentage changes, never absolute counts. Two publications with strong prior-period counts showed no transactions in the current window, consistent with a change in billing platform rather than subscriber loss; they were excluded from rankings rather than reported as declines. We never share customer-identifiable information. For questions about how we use data in anonymized or aggregated form for trend reporting, email privacy@brex.com.

title: Shift at Midnight Single Player: Can You Play Solo? (Plus a Free Solo Alternative)
summary: Yes, Shift at Midnight has a single-player mode - but it's built for co-op. Here's how solo really plays, plus a free solo skinwalker game in your browser.
body_text: The clips that made Shift at Midnight famous all have the same soundtrack: three people yelling at each other over proximity chat about whether the man at the counter has too many teeth. Which raises the obvious question for everyone without a horror group chat - can you play Shift at Midnight single player? Short answer: yes. Longer answer: it is a different game, and it is harder in ways the design did not really intend. Yes, Shift at Midnight supports solo play The game is listed as online co-op for 1-3 players, and that 1 is real - you can start a shift alone. Nothing is locked behind having a party, and the full run of nights is playable by yourself. A post-launch update even widened lobbies beyond three, but the developer has been clear the game is designed and balanced around three players. What solo actually feels like You are doing every job at once. Register, ID verification, records lookup, and watching the doors are four responsibilities that were meant to be split. Nobody covers the back. When something gets past you, there is no second player to board a door while you hide. You lose proximity chat, which is a bigger deal than it sounds - a large share of the game's tension and comedy lives in hearing a friend panic two aisles away. The upside: pure dread. No one is cracking jokes to break the atmosphere. Solo is genuinely scarier, just less fun to clip. If you want the intended experience, play with two other people. If you want a horror game that was built from the ground up for one person, that is a different recommendation. A free single-player skinwalker game, built solo-first Six Midnight Shifts is a free browser game inspired by Shift at Midnight and designed as single-player from the start. There is no co-op to miss, because the whole loop is balanced for one pair of hands: serve impatient customers, keep the store running, compare each face and answer against county records, and use the sidearm under the counter only when you are certain the person in front of you is not a person. Play Six Midnight Shifts free - no download, no lobby, no friends required. Six nights, and they get worse. Solo tips that carry across both games Verify in a fixed order every single time. Improvising is how you miss a mismatch. Trust the records over the customer. The thing at your counter is better at lying than you are at reading faces. Do the mundane tasks between customers, never during. Split attention is what kills solo players. Hesitating costs you less than being wrong. Take the extra second. Frequently asked questions Can you play Shift at Midnight alone? Yes. It supports 1-3 players, so a solo run is fully playable - but the game is balanced around three. Is Shift at Midnight harder solo? Yes. You handle every role yourself, and there is nobody to barricade doors or distract a creature while you deal with the counter. Does Shift at Midnight have offline single player? It is an online co-op game that you can play by yourself; treat it as a solo online session rather than a dedicated offline mode. What is the best single-player alternative? Six Midnight Shifts, a free browser skinwalker horror game built specifically for one player. See our free-to-play guide . title: Dragonfly Energy Partners with Sphere Energy to Develop Next-Generation AI-Enhanced Battery Technology
summary: First battery pack manufacturer to embed Sphere Energy’s AI-powered state-of-health technology into its core BMS architecture Sphere Energy’s proprietary battery AI models will be integrated into Dragonfly Energy’s next-generation battery management system architecture.
body_text: Dragonfly Energy Partners with Sphere Energy to Develop Next-Generation AI-Enhanced Battery Technology August 17, 2026 PDF Version First battery pack manufacturer to embed Sphere Energy’s AI-powered state-of-health technology into its core BMS architecture Sphere Energy’s proprietary battery AI models will be integrated into Dragonfly Energy’s next-generation battery management system architecture. The integration is designed to improve state-of-charge and state-of-health accuracy while expanding Dragonfly IntelLigence® into AI-enhanced battery management. The partnership will leverage Dragonfly Energy’s hundreds of thousands of deployed battery packs, established OEM relationships and vertically integrated engineering capabilities to accelerate data-driven product development. RENO, Nev., Aug. 17, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Dragonfly Energy Holdings Corp. (Nasdaq: DFLI) (“Dragonfly Energy” or the “Company”), an industry leader in energy storage, today announced a strategic partnership with Sphere Energy to develop and integrate next-generation AI capabilities into its future battery technologies and integrated power systems. With hundreds of thousands of battery packs deployed across a broad range of applications, Dragonfly Energy has built a substantial base of real-world operating data spanning years of field performance. The partnership will combine that data with Sphere Energy’s battery-specific AI technology, based on its AI platform VETTA®, advancing the Company’s Dragonfly IntelLigence® communications technology beyond battery connectivity and system visibility and creating an AI-driven intelligence layer across future products and systems. Sphere Energy’s proprietary battery AI models will be integrated into Dragonfly Energy’s next-generation battery management system architecture, making Dragonfly Energy the first battery pack manufacturer to place Sphere Energy’s AI-powered state-of-health technology at its core. The integration is designed to improve the accuracy of state-of-charge and state-of-health data while creating a more flexible development platform that can help Dragonfly Energy bring new products and solutions to market faster in response to specific customer needs. “Our established product lines, long-standing customer relationships and years of field performance have created a powerful data advantage,” said Dr. Denis Phares, chief executive officer of Dragonfly Energy. “By combining that data advantage with Sphere Energy’s battery-specific AI models, we expect to evolve Dragonfly IntelLigence into a platform capable of delivering more precise, actionable insights across the applications we serve.” “Dragonfly Energy’s vertically integrated capabilities, substantial deployed base and established relationships with leading OEM customers provide a unique foundation for applying battery-specific artificial intelligence at scale,” said Luca Scherrer, co-founder and managing director of Sphere Energy. “That combination gives us the opportunity to apply our technology across a broad range of real-world applications and operating conditions, turning battery data into better intelligence, stronger product performance and greater value for customers.” For fleet operators, OEMs and other commercial customers, more accurate battery intelligence is intended to provide greater visibility into battery condition and lifecycle performance, supporting better asset management and operating decisions. The AI-enabled architecture is also designed to create a faster feedback loop between field performance and product development, helping Dragonfly Energy refine existing products and accelerate future solutions. Together, we believe these capabilities can turn Dragonfly Energy’s growing base of field data into a lasting advantage across product performance, development and customer value. Dr. Lukas Lutz, a director of Dragonfly Energy is also a co-founder of Sphere Energy. For more information about Dragonfly Energy, visit Dragonflyenergy.com. About Dragonfly Energy Dragonfly Energy Holdings Corp. (Nasdaq: DFLI) is a comprehensive lithium battery technology company, specializing in cell manufacturing, battery pack assembly, and full system integration. Through its renowned Battle Born Batteries® brand, Dragonfly Energy has established itself as a frontrunner in the lithium battery industry, with hundreds of thousands of reliable battery packs deployed in the field through top-tier OEMs and a diverse retail customer base. At the forefront of domestic lithium battery cell production, Dragonfly Energy’s patented dry electrode manufacturing process can deliver chemistry-agnostic power solutions for a broad spectrum of applications, including energy storage systems, electric vehicles, and consumer electronics. The Company’s overarching mission is the future deployment of its proprietary, nonflammable, all-solid-state battery cells. To learn more about Dragonfly Energy and its commitment to clean energy advancements, visit investors.dragonflyenergy.com .
